journeys.label: Analyst publishing their own work
journeys.sub: Free membership. Writes with the engine, publishes under their own name, keeps half of what it sells for — and reads rivals in exchange for scoring them.

nodes.label: The analyst programme page
nodes.sees: 'Your report. Your name on it. Half of what it earns.' Free membership, a fresh report every month, they set the price, they keep 50% of every sale, and a public dated track record anyone can check.
nodes.behind: The terms page is the binding version: ownership, the 50/50 split, how payment works, takedown, and what happens if they leave.

nodes.label: Signs in with LinkedIn
nodes.sees: One button. Signing in is also how they accept the analyst terms. A link to their LinkedIn profile is required before they can publish anything.
nodes.behind: Analyst is a role on the same account as a member subscription — someone can be both, and then keeps the better of each allowance.
nodes.gap: Today any LinkedIn sign-in becomes an analyst. There is no approval step, and that is a known blocker before this goes live.

nodes.label: Analyst workspace
nodes.sees: The member area in analyst mode: this month's generation, other analysts' reports to read and score, their own published work, and the income panel.
nodes.behind: One open publishing obligation at a time. Until the last generation is published, the next one is locked — and that carries across months.
nodes.gap: An analyst who has been banned simply cannot start a generation, with nothing on screen explaining why.

nodes.label: Start from what?
nodes.sees: Either generate a fresh report on a company of their choice, or build on another analyst's published analysis — pay that analyst's price plus a €10 fee and start from their work.
nodes.behind: A fork is copied as its own order with its own revision budget and no inherited file, so revising it can never overwrite the original that everyone else is reading.

nodes.label: Starts this month's report
nodes.sees: They pick a company and start. A banner warns that this commits them to publishing it under their own name.
nodes.behind: The monthly slot and the publishing obligation are taken together, before the engine starts. If the generation fails outright, both are given back.

nodes.label: Builds on another analysis
nodes.sees: 'Build on this' on a published analysis. One payment covers the other analyst's price plus a €10 derivation fee, and they land in their own copy to reprompt.
nodes.behind: The original analyst gets half of the price part; the €10 is Valuatum's. A fork must be revised or edited by hand at least once before it can be published — an untouched fork is just the original. Someone who is not an analyst can fork too, and then owes no publication at all.
nodes.gap: The buy-or-fork chooser is still a browser prompt box asking you to type 1 or 2.
dev: server/lambda/members.js:1202 — revised or edited before publishing

nodes.label: Engine writes it · 20–40 min
nodes.sees: Progress in the workspace; an email when it is done.
nodes.behind: Same queue and engine as every other report.

nodes.label: Steers it — revisions or hand edits
nodes.sees: The order page, where they either reprompt the report in plain language (€5 a round beyond the plan) or open 'Edit the report text' and rewrite paragraphs themselves, free and as often as they like. This is where the analyst's actual judgement goes in.
nodes.behind: The comments they type, and the paragraphs they rewrite, are in effect the published work — the engine writes, the analyst directs. A later AI revision keeps hand-edited paragraphs word for word. They can choose to show their prompts publicly, which puts a 'steered with…' teaser on the company page.

nodes.label: Publishes it
nodes.sees: They set a price in euros and how many days until it becomes free to read, then publish. It goes out under their own name. The price can be changed later from the same list.
nodes.behind: Company, recommendation and target price are taken from the delivered report, never from the browser, so the listing cannot be gamed. Publishing freezes that PDF — no more revisions, no more hand edits, and no more rounds to buy. Publishing is also what releases the obligation, so the next monthly generation opens.
nodes.gap: Nothing is reviewed before it goes public; moderation happens afterwards.

nodes.label: Steps down instead
nodes.sees: 'Continue without publishing' turns them into an ordinary reader. The report they generated stays private and theirs.
nodes.behind: Refused while a publication is still owed — they cannot walk away from an open obligation.
nodes.gap: That leaves one genuinely stuck state: an obligation that is open but cannot be met needs an admin to clear it by hand.

nodes.label: Live on the company page
nodes.sees: Their analysis appears in the analyst section of that company's page, with their name on it, and in the member area for other members to read.
nodes.behind: Anyone can buy it — no account needed. Buyers get an email with a permanent link. After the free-after date it opens to everyone.
nodes.gap: Rendering a published analysis onto the company page is the piece still being finished.

nodes.label: Published, no sales yet
nodes.sees: It sits on the company page building their public track record, and members can read it.
nodes.behind: The next monthly generation is unlocked either way — publishing is what counts, not selling. Each paying member who reads it earns them a flat €0.50 (held 14 days like a sale); reads by other analysts and by free readers earn nothing.
dev: server/lambda/members.js:1845-1852 — only a subscriber's read pays

nodes.label: Someone buys it
nodes.sees: A reader — or another analyst forking it — pays the price the analyst set.
nodes.behind: The buyer gets an emailed permanent link that re-checks the payment.

nodes.label: Taken down by an admin
nodes.sees: The analysis disappears from the public page and the reader is refunded.
nodes.behind: Moderation is after the fact: an admin can take anything down, which voids the sale and claws back the earning. An admin can also reopen it, which puts the publishing obligation back.
nodes.gap: There is no admin screen for this yet — it is an API call.

nodes.label: Income panel
nodes.sees: Four figures: paid to you, ready to invoice, held for 14 days, and what your reports sold for — plus a line and a row per subscriber read. Under them, how the money works.
nodes.behind: Half of every sale is theirs, and a flat €0.50 per read by a paying member, both held 14 days to cover chargebacks and moderation, after which they invoice Valuatum. There is no automatic payout.
nodes.gap: Analysts invoice by hand — no Stripe Connect, no payroll integration.

nodes.label: Invoices — and the record grows
nodes.sees: They invoice for what has cleared. Being free to write again is not part of this step: that happened the moment they published. The only wait left is the calendar — one free generation per month, so the next opens on the 1st.
nodes.behind: The publish obligation is cleared on submit, and the monthly slot is a calendar-month flag. An analyst who never publishes stays blocked however long they wait; an admin can clear the obligation by hand. Their public track record grows with every published report, which is the point of the programme.

nodes.label: Other analysts' reports
nodes.sees: A list of what other analysts have published, filtered by ticker, with each one's peer score. Analysts get 20 of these reads a month, free — that is the trade.
nodes.behind: This is the read-and-score loop that ranks analysts. Reading is free, but each read has to be paid for with a score.

nodes.label: Opens one — a read is spent
nodes.sees: The analysis opens, with the other analyst's steering prompts shown next to it so they can judge what was actually added.
nodes.behind: Opening it spends one read and puts them under an obligation to score it. Re-opening the same one later is free.

nodes.label: Scores it: 1–5 and why
nodes.sees: A score from 1 to 5 and at least 40 characters on what this added over the plain engine report, or over the other takes on the same company. Anything shorter is refused.
nodes.behind: Only one unscored analysis at a time. Scores can be corrected later from 'My reviews', which keeps the old value in the history.

nodes.label: Ranking updated, next read open
nodes.sees: The analysis's peer score moves and their next read is unlocked.
nodes.behind: The ranking is deliberately forgiving: a new analysis starts from a neutral prior, more reviews count for more, and age pulls a score down slowly — so one bad score cannot bury someone.
nodes.gap: If that analyst later takes coverage of the same company, their scores of rivals on it are silently voided — the rival's score drops with no notice to anyone.

nodes.label: Free to read — nothing owed
nodes.sees: The analysis is past its free-after date, or in a free window we opened. It just opens.
nodes.behind: No read is spent and no score is owed. This is also how someone with no account at all can read a published analysis.

nodes.label: Blocked — score the last one first
nodes.sees: 'Score and comment the analysis you opened last before opening another.'
nodes.behind: Exactly one unscored analysis may be open at a time. There is no way to skip it — the only ways out are to score it, stop reading, or step down to being an ordinary reader.

nodes.label: Refused — they cover that company
nodes.sees: 'Buy it instead' — an analyst who covers a company cannot spend a free read on a rival's take on it.
nodes.behind: This keeps competitors from grading each other for free. They can still buy it like anyone else.

nodes.label: Suspended — bounced back to sign-in
nodes.sees: Nothing that explains anything. The workspace never loads: they are signed out and land back on the sign-in screen. Signing in again works, and drops them straight back out.
nodes.behind: A suspended account is refused on every call. The page treats that refusal the same as an expired session, so it clears the login and reloads — which is why it loops.
nodes.gap: A suspended analyst is never told they are suspended, and there is no way for them to ask why. Telling that refusal apart from an expired session is a small change on the page.

journeys.label: Anyone buying a report
journeys.sub: No account. Finds a company page, pays, gets a PDF by email.

options.label: Open a free report + buy revisions
Ask us to cover a company

nodes.label: Company report page
nodes.sees: A page about one company: overview, risks, a free sample if there is one, and the buttons that start every purchase — Download free PDF, Buy ready report — €20, Generate fresh report — €50, and Analyst reports. The buttons carry the live price. People arrive from Google, from the Reports catalog, or from the site search.
nodes.behind: These pages are built in advance for about 1,200 companies. The catalog at reports.html shows the same choices as cards. The blog, the comparison pages, the A–Z company index and the author pages all funnel here; none of them sells anything itself.

nodes.label: They choose…
nodes.sees: Open a free PDF; buy a ready report (already written, downloads instantly, €20, or €25 with two revision requests); order a fresh report (written on demand, about 30 minutes, €50, or €55 with two revisions); buy an analysis a named analyst published on this company; or, if we do not cover the company at all, ask us to add it. On a free report the only thing for sale is a set of three revisions for €10.
nodes.behind: Prices come from Stripe when the page loads, so every page shows the same price, and each revision tier carries its own included count. Every checkout on the site is built in one place and accepts promo codes.
dev: api/pricing.js + server/stripe-pricing.js — live prices and included counts
server/checkout.js — every Stripe checkout the shop sells

nodes.label: Reads the free PDF
nodes.sees: The PDF opens straight away. No email, no payment, no account. Next to the download there is one paid button: 'Create a revision — €10', for when they want the report changed — a different assumption, a scenario.
nodes.behind: Free reports are ordinary links to the file store. A few rotate into the free tier each week to bring in search traffic; the rest cannot be opened without paying, even if someone guesses the address. The revision button is baked hidden and only appears once live pricing confirms the free-revisions tier is on sale.
dev: api/create-checkout.js — a free report itself cannot be sold, only its revisions

nodes.label: Done — has the PDF
nodes.sees: Nothing more. The page and the button stay there, so revisions can be bought any time later.

nodes.label: Pays on the Stripe page
nodes.sees: A payment page hosted by Stripe showing the report and the price. They fill in their email and card, or use Google/Apple Pay, and can enter a promo code. The email typed here is where the report will be sent.
nodes.behind: Before this page opens, the site checks the report really is for sale, and — for the revisions option — that this report can be revised at all. Everything the later steps need (which company, ready, fresh or free, revisions or not) travels with the payment. For a free report the checkout is the 'free-revisions' kind: €10 for three revision requests, the PDF they already have.
dev: the screenshot is an illustration; a real Stripe page needs a live session

nodes.label: Picks an analyst's analysis
nodes.sees: The analyst section of the company page lists what named analysts have published on it, with their peer score and price. Two buttons: buy it, or — for another analyst — build on it.
nodes.behind: No account is needed to buy one. Reports that have passed their free-after date are simply readable, with nothing to pay.

nodes.label: Pays the analyst's price
nodes.sees: A Stripe page for that analysis, at the price the analyst set. Someone building on it instead pays that price plus a €10 fee.
nodes.behind: Half of the price goes to the analyst who wrote it; the €10 derivation fee is Valuatum's.

nodes.label: Opens the analysis
nodes.sees: They come back to the company page and the analysis opens in a new tab. An email arrives with a permanent link.
nodes.behind: The link re-checks the payment each time, so it can be kept and used later. Someone who forked rather than bought lands in their own copy instead and can reprompt it.

nodes.label: Asks us to cover a company
nodes.sees: A form at the bottom of the catalog: up to 200 company names, one per line, plus an email and an optional note. Institutions have their own version of the same form on the Institutions page, asking about volume and API access.
nodes.behind: Both forms send us an email and nothing else. There is no automatic reply, no ticket, and no way for the person to check what happened — someone has to pick it up by hand.
nodes.gap: This is a lead that lands in an inbox. Nothing tells the person we received it, and nothing tells us later that the company they asked for is now covered.

nodes.label: Checkout cancelled
nodes.sees: A short 'Checkout cancelled' page with a way back to the catalog. Nothing was charged.
nodes.behind: Nothing was saved — no order, not even the email address.
nodes.gap: There is no reminder email for an abandoned checkout, because there is nothing to send it to.

nodes.label: Payment recorded
nodes.sees: Nothing — this happens in the second after paying, while they are being sent to the thank-you page.
nodes.behind: Stripe tells the site the payment succeeded, and the purchase is saved with the buyer's email. A ready report is emailed at once; a fresh report becomes an order and the writing starts; revisions on a free report become an order with three rounds and the PDF already delivered. If saving fails, Stripe keeps retrying until it works, and the same payment is never recorded twice.

nodes.label: Thank-you page
nodes.sees: For a ready report: 'Payment confirmed' and a Download button. For a fresh report: 'Order confirmed', arriving by email in about 30 minutes. If revisions were bought there is also a 'Track order & request a revision' link — that link is the only way into the order page. For revisions on a free report the page says 'Revisions added' and leads with 'Request a revision', since the PDF was already theirs.
nodes.behind: The page asks Stripe whether this payment really went through before showing anything. The download button does not point at the file; it goes through the site, which re-checks the payment on every click.

nodes.label: Email: order confirmed
nodes.sees: 'Order confirmed' — we are writing your report, it will arrive in about 30 minutes. With revisions, this email also carries the 'Track your order' link.
nodes.behind: Only a confirmation. The report itself comes in a second email when it is finished.

nodes.label: Email: your report
nodes.sees: 'Your report is ready' with a Download PDF button — and a 'Request revision' link only if revision rounds were bought.
nodes.behind: The download button uses the same gated link as the thank-you page, so the email keeps working later.
nodes.gap: Someone who bought without revisions gets no revision link at all, so there is no way for them to buy rounds afterwards. Adding that link for every buyer is a small change in the same email.

nodes.label: Email: your revisions
nodes.sees: 'Your revisions are ready to use' with a 'Request a revision' button and, underneath, a courtesy link to the PDF they already had. The subject says revisions, not report.
nodes.behind: The same delivery email as a ready report, switched into its revisions-only form because the checkout was of the free-revisions kind.

nodes.label: Report is written · ~30 min
nodes.sees: Nothing, unless they bought revisions and opened the order page — there it says 'Preparing your report…'.
nodes.behind: A background worker imports the company's latest financial data, then asks the report engine to write and lay out the PDF, checking back every few minutes until it is done. If the data import times out it simply tries again next round.
dev: server/lambda/worker.js — runs every 5 minutes and on demand

nodes.label: Downloads the PDF
nodes.sees: The PDF opens or downloads, from the thank-you page or from the email.
nodes.behind: Every download makes a fresh, short-lived link after checking the payment again. There is no permanent file address for a paid ready report.

nodes.label: Email: your report
nodes.sees: 'Your report is ready' with a Download button. This link is permanent and can be used any time later.
nodes.behind: The finished PDF is stored privately and does not appear in the public catalog unless resale is switched on. The email is sent exactly once, even if the worker crashes half-way.

nodes.label: Report could not be written
nodes.sees: An email: 'We couldn't finish your report' — something went wrong, the team has been told, and they will either get the report at this address once it is fixed or hear about a refund. They need do nothing. The order page, if they have the link, says the same.
nodes.behind: After the last retry the order is marked failed. The customer is emailed first, then we get an alert that says whether that email went out, so someone can generate the report by hand or refund. Every engine failure reaches us this way; the retries in between are silent after the first.

nodes.label: Done — has the report
nodes.sees: Nothing more. Without the revisions option there is no order page and no way to ask for changes.
nodes.behind: The purchase stays recorded and the emailed link keeps working.
nodes.gap: This is the most common ending, and it is a dead end: no upsell, no way to buy revisions later.

nodes.label: Order page
nodes.sees: 'Your report is ready' with the Download button, an 'Edit the report text' button, a box to describe a change in plain language, how many revision rounds are left, and the version history. While the report is still being written it says 'Preparing your report…' and refreshes itself.
nodes.behind: Reachable only through the link in the thank-you page and the emails — the link carries the payment reference. The page refreshes every 8 seconds. Members reach the same page from the member area with their login instead. Editing by hand is free and unlimited on any delivered version; asking the AI for a revision uses a round.

nodes.label: Done — has the report
nodes.sees: Nothing more. Without revisions there is no order page; the emailed link is permanent.
nodes.behind: The PDF stays stored privately. After the resale window (14 days) it is hidden from any resale listing, but the customer's link keeps working.

nodes.label: Done — keeps the link
nodes.sees: Nothing more. The order page and the emailed link keep working, unused revision rounds stay available, and the text can be edited by hand at any time.

nodes.label: Asks for a revision
nodes.sees: They type the change in plain language — for example 'assume the gold price doubles in 2027' — and press Request revision. The page switches to 'Revising your report…'.
nodes.behind: The request is checked (not empty, not absurdly long) and one revision round is reserved. If none are left, the page offers to buy more at €5 per round. An AI revision keeps any paragraphs they edited by hand word for word.

nodes.label: No rounds left — offered more
nodes.sees: 'You've used all included revisions', with a Buy more revision rounds button. That opens a small Stripe payment (€5 per round, 1–10 at a time) and returns them to the same page with the rounds added.
nodes.behind: Extra rounds are a separate small purchase attached to the same order.

nodes.label: Report is revised · ~30 min
nodes.sees: 'Revising your report…' on the order page.
nodes.behind: The engine takes the original report plus the customer's comment and produces a new version, with a short memo of what changed — target price, rating, forecasts. The original file is never overwritten.

nodes.label: Revision failed — round given back
nodes.sees: An email: 'Your revision couldn't be completed' — the current report is unchanged, the round was not counted, and an 'Open your order' button to try again. The order page shows the same message in a banner.
nodes.behind: The order goes back to delivered with its previous PDF and the round is given back. A requested revision may have been waiting for hours, so it is emailed; a hand edit that fails is only shown on the page the customer is watching. Either way we get an alert.

nodes.label: Email: report updated
nodes.sees: 'Your report has been updated', with a Download button for the new version and a link back to the order page.
nodes.behind: Sent once the revised PDF is stored. Every version keeps its own permanent link.

nodes.label: New version on the order page
nodes.sees: The version history now shows 'Version 2 · AI revision' at the top: what they asked for, what moved (target price, rating, forecasts) and a download link per version. If rounds remain they can ask again, and they can edit the text by hand at any time.
nodes.behind: One round is now used. The history stays with the order.

nodes.label: Edits the text by hand
nodes.sees: 'Edit the report text' opens the report as it will print, right on the order page. They click a paragraph, change the wording, and the panel on the right lists every change word by word with a live page-fit estimate. They can add their name for the byline, then press 'Save as a new version'. Headings, figures, tables and charts cannot be changed.
nodes.behind: The engine's rendered HTML is shown in a sandboxed frame, every editable paragraph tagged with a pointer. The edits go to the engine, which re-renders the PDF with the new text in seconds — no AI pass. The engine warns when an edit changes a number in prose (the tables are not updated) and when a page no longer fits.

nodes.label: Re-rendered · seconds
nodes.sees: 'Revising your report…' for a moment, then the page refreshes.
nodes.behind: The order goes DELIVERED → REVISING with the pending edit on the row; the worker sends the edits to the engine, polls, and delivers the new version. No email is sent, no round is used, and the edit counts as a change of their own for anything that needs one. If the render fails, the page shows the error and the previous version stays — no email, since they are watching.

nodes.label: New version — 'Edited by hand'
nodes.sees: The version history shows 'Version 2 · Edited by hand — Written by ⟨name⟩', with each edited paragraph before and after, and a download link per version. If they changed a figure in the text, a note says the tables were not updated.
nodes.behind: Every history entry now records who wrote it: the original delivery and AI revisions are 'AI-written', a hand edit carries the name, and an AI revision on top of hand edits says which paragraphs it kept. Versions stay linear — an edit always builds on the newest one.

journeys.label: Member on a monthly plan
journeys.sub: Pays every month for picks from the catalog, their own generations, and other analysts' work.

options.label: Take a report from the library

nodes.label: Pricing page
nodes.sees: Four plans side by side: Investor €19/month, Investor Plus €39/month, Company Coverage €59 per company per year (up to five companies), and the free analyst membership. Each lists how many catalog reports, generations, analyst reads and revision rounds it includes.
nodes.behind: The limits shown here are the real numbers the system enforces later. Picking a plan here remembers it, so after signing in they are offered 'Continue to checkout' straight away.

nodes.label: Signs in
nodes.sees: Two ways in, side by side: analysts sign in with LinkedIn, subscribers type their email and get a sign-in link. No passwords anywhere.
nodes.behind: The emailed link works for 15 minutes. There is no password to lose or reset.
nodes.gap: Anyone who signs in with LinkedIn currently becomes an analyst — there is no gate on that yet.

nodes.label: Pays for the plan
nodes.sees: A Stripe page for the monthly or yearly subscription. After paying they land back in the member area with the plan active.
nodes.behind: The subscription's state comes from Stripe. A failed card leaves the plan working in a grace period; a cancellation ends it at once.
nodes.gap: There is no self-service upgrade, downgrade or cancel — those are emails to support today.
dev: members.js:127 — past_due still counts as active

nodes.label: Member area
nodes.sees: One page, not tabs: a strip at the top with their email, plan and how much of each allowance is left, then the report library, other analysts' reports, the monthly generation, buying an extra report, and — for analysts — income.
nodes.behind: Which sections appear depends on the plan and the role. The counters are a per-month record; everything resets on the 1st.

nodes.label: Plan ended — what they keep
nodes.sees: The plans come back and the allowances are gone. Reports they already have still open; anything the subscription paid for says the subscription is not active.
nodes.behind: A failed card keeps working during a grace period; a cancellation drops the tier immediately. One-off purchases and their own generations stay theirs forever. Library picks survive only while a LinkedIn role does.
nodes.gap: Nothing warns anyone before this happens, and there is no self-service way to resubscribe from inside the member area.

nodes.label: They choose…
nodes.sees: Take one of this month's picks from the catalog, generate a fresh report on a company they choose, buy an extra report beyond the plan, open another analyst's published analysis, or — on Company Coverage — ask for an update on a company they cover.
nodes.behind: Each draws on a different allowance and each is counted separately.

nodes.label: Takes a library pick
nodes.sees: A list of catalog reports they can claim this month. Opening one they already took costs nothing.
nodes.behind: Only reports older than 30 days can be picked, so the newest work stays paid-for. Investor gets 3 a month, Investor Plus 10. A report that happens to be in the free rotation costs no pick at all.

nodes.label: Uses the monthly generation
nodes.sees: They pick any listed company and start a report. Investor Plus includes one a month; the plain Investor plan includes none.
nodes.behind: The monthly slot is reserved before the engine starts, so a failure never silently eats it — a failed generation gives the month back.

nodes.label: Buys an extra report
nodes.sees: 'Another report, on demand' — €40 for members instead of the €50 list price. Paid through Stripe, then it behaves like any fresh report.
nodes.behind: The member price is worked out on the server from their live subscription, not from anything the browser sends.

nodes.label: Asks for a coverage update
nodes.sees: Company Coverage subscribers get a card per company they cover, with a Request an update button and a confirmation dialog. Four updates per company per year, on top of the latest existing report.
nodes.behind: The update is a private generation for that company. It comes with no revision rounds at all.
nodes.gap: Asking for a company that is not on the subscription is refused, and so is a year with all four updates used — both as bare error messages.

nodes.label: Opens an analyst's analysis
nodes.sees: Another analyst's published work, included in the plan — 5 reads a month on Investor, 20 on Investor Plus. The analyst's own steering prompts are shown alongside it.
nodes.behind: Opening one spends a read. An analysis inside a free window costs no read at all.

nodes.label: Has to score it first
nodes.sees: Before they can open another one, they must give this analysis a score from 1 to 5 and write at least 40 characters on what it added over the plain engine report.
nodes.behind: Only one unscored analysis can be open at a time — the next open is refused until this one is scored. Those scores are what rank analysts against each other.

nodes.label: Scored — next read unlocked
nodes.sees: The score is theirs to change later from 'My reviews'. They can open the next analysis.
nodes.behind: A subscriber's read also pays the analyst who wrote it €0.50.
nodes.gap: The analyst workspace still says member reads are not counted yet, which the code contradicts — the €0.50 per read is live.

nodes.label: Allowance used up — can top up
nodes.sees: The counter that ran out offers a top-up: €5 for an extra report pick, €2 for an extra analyst read, up to 20 at a time. A used-up monthly generation just says so and waits for the 1st.
nodes.behind: Top-ups are added to the same monthly record, so anything bought and not used expires at the end of the month. A plan with none of that allowance at all cannot top it up.
nodes.gap: Buying credits late in the month can mean paying for something that expires days later — nothing warns about that.

nodes.label: Report is written · 20–40 min
nodes.sees: The card shows progress and refreshes by itself; they can close the page.
nodes.behind: Member generations go through exactly the same queue and engine as everything a non-member orders. A failure is emailed to them and to us, like any fresh report.

nodes.label: Reads it
nodes.sees: The report opens. It stays theirs — re-opening later does not spend another pick.
nodes.behind: A claimed report is recorded against the account, so the entitlement outlives the month it was claimed in.

nodes.label: Email: your report
nodes.sees: 'Your report is ready' with a permanent download link, same as any other buyer gets.

nodes.label: Order page
nodes.sees: The same order page a non-member gets, reached from the member area. It shows the download, an 'Edit the report text' button, the revision box and how many rounds the plan includes — 2 on Investor Plus, none on Investor, none at all on a coverage update.
nodes.behind: The page uses their login instead of a payment reference. Extra rounds beyond the plan cost €5 each, bought 1–10 at a time. Editing by hand is free and unlimited, and the byline is always the member's own name.

nodes.label: Revised report
nodes.sees: The new version appears in the revision history with a note of what changed.
nodes.behind: Same revision machinery as every other order.

nodes.label: Done for this month
nodes.sees: Their allowances tick down; everything resets on the 1st.
nodes.behind: Reports already delivered stay reachable through their links even if the subscription later ends.
nodes.gap: Unused picks, reads and generations do not roll over.

nodes.label: Sign-in did not work
nodes.sees: Either 'LinkedIn sign-in was cancelled', or — for a sign-in link that has expired or already been used — 'Sign-in failed: Invalid or expired link'. The sign-in cards are still there, so they can ask for another link.
nodes.behind: A sign-in link lives 15 minutes and works once. Asking for a new one always answers 'if the address is valid, a link is on its way', so a typed-wrong address looks exactly like a correct one.
nodes.gap: Nothing tells someone their link has simply gone stale in their inbox; the message reads like a failure on their part.

nodes.label: Hand-edited version
nodes.sees: The new version appears in the history as 'Edited by hand — Written by ⟨their name⟩', with every changed paragraph before and after. No round was used.
nodes.behind: Same editing machinery as every other order; the members API routes it under their generation.
